gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a '3000' inverter is not a 3,000 W continuous load rating across brands. Victron rates its MultiPlus-II 12/3000/120-50 at 3,000 VA, which is 2,400 W at 25 °C, 2,200 W at 40 °C and 1,700 W at 65 °C, with a 5,500 W peak. On the Renogy store text I read, Renogy rates its 12V 3000W inverter at '3000W continuous / 6000W peak' and the REGO 12V 3000W at 'peak power up to 9000W', with no temperature or surge duration given.
standout_why: I compared against the cited Victron knowledge article 'How to Size a Solar System for Your RV'. Its only inverter figure is an allowance of 'about 10-15% extra' for inverter losses. It has no VA vs W, no temperature derating, no surge duration and no idle draw. I tried to open the cited Renogy 'RV Inverter Installation Guide' but got only site navigation (6,858 characters, no article body). I tried to open rvtime.com but it failed on an SSL certificate error. ChatGPT's own answer sizes by headline watts ('3,000W … larger microwave, multiple appliances, some air conditioners') and treats the Renogy $414.99 3000W and $949 REGO cards as like-for-like 3,000 W units.
decides: It changes the sizing advice more than the brand pick. A 3,000-class inverter in a hot RV bay should be planned at about 2,200 W continuous, using Victron's 40 °C figure, because Renogy publishes no temperature basis. Someone running an RV air conditioner or a microwave plus a coffee maker on a 'starter 2,000W' unit is likely under-sized. The surge figures also don't compare: Renogy's 6,000 W and 9,000 W 'peak' carry no duration on the store text, while Victron's 5,500 W peak sits beside a continuous rating that drops with temperature. Idle draw matters for solar-only RV use. Victron states 13 W at zero load, 9 W in AES mode and 3 W in Search mode. That is about 312 Wh/day at 13 W versus 72 Wh/day at 3 W, roughly a third of a 100 W panel's daily yield. I could not source the Renogy equivalents, so the idle comparison is one-sided.
